title: Two sugars, one big family
question: What sets DNA and RNA apart from each other?
hook: They are built from the same kind of parts, yet one small swap changes which molecule you have.
idea: DNA and RNA are both chains of nucleotides, told apart by their sugar and by one base.

beats.prompt: Match each item to its partner.
beats.explain: The sugar decides the polymer, and thymine and uracil split between the two.

beats.prompt: Sort each feature into the nucleic acid it describes.
beats.explain: Sugar, one base and usual strand count all separate the two.

beats.prompt: You test a virus and find its genome is double-stranded RNA. Is that possible?

choices.label: No, RNA is always single-stranded
choices.feedback: RNA is usually single-stranded, which makes this tempting, but there are exceptions.

choices.label: Yes, some viruses have double-stranded RNA genomes
No, viruses have no nucleic acids at all
choices.feedback: Viruses do contain nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA.

beats.explain: Natural RNA is usually single-stranded, but some viruses have genomes made of double-stranded RNA.

beats.prompt: Put these discoveries in order, earliest first.
items: Altmann coins the term nucleic acid
Astbury and Bell publish the first X-ray pattern of DNA
Watson and Crick propose the double helix
